summary: The paper evaluates a one-pass out-of-fold filter. It runs 5-fold cross-validated logistic regression, drops every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refits. It is tested on digits and breast cancer with synthetic symmetric noise at 20% and 40%, over 5 seeds. It reports gains over noisy logistic regression on digits (recovery 78% and 68%), a smaller and less certain gain on breast cancer, large wins over a default MLP, a small cost on clean labels, and 65-76% precision of the dropped samples. The paper is candid about its limits, but the comparisons that could show the method is useful are mostly missing.
strengths: Claims are scoped honestly. The paper states where the claim stops (breast cancer at 40%), calls the MLP comparison weak, and lists the missing baselines and untested hyperparameters.
Paired per-seed differences are reported alongside means and sds. The baseline is paired on the same split and noisy labels, which is a sound design for such a small study.

Because the noise is synthetic, the paper can measure what the filter drops (precision, recall, share of the training set removed, Fig. 2). It also shows the cost on clean labels and the over-dropping of clean samples, rather than only the headline gain.
The method is simple and fully specified (K=5, C=1, no tuning), and the settings are stated.
The realized noise rates and the recovery definition are reported, and the paper says recovery is unstable when the loss is small.

weaknesses.issue: The decisive baseline is missing. The only reference is logistic regression at a single fixed C=1, and the only other model is an untuned MLP trained on noisy labels. Strong L2 regularization (small C) is the standard, nearly free defence of a linear model against symmetric noise. Without it the 6-9 point gains on digits may only show that C=1 is a poor setting under noise. The filter also uses C=1 for its out-of-fold models, so the filter's own sensitivity to C is untested. The text concedes this ('whether stronger L2 regularization closes much of the gap is open'), but the abstract, title and contribution list still present the gain as the main result.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add logistic regression over a grid of C (for example 1e-3 to 1e2, selected on the noisy labels by cross-validation, which needs no clean data), and report the filter at a few C values. If that is impossible, state in the abstract and the first contribution that the gain is relative to an untuned C=1 model, and soften 'improves on logistic regression'. The wins over the MLP should not be a headline contribution (the third bullet in Sec. 1).

weaknesses.issue: The novelty and the closest baselines are not tested. The method is Wilson-style editing with a cross-validated linear classifier. Confident learning (the paper's closest relative) and Wilson editing are cited but not run, although both are a few lines with off-the-shelf tools. The paper therefore cannot say whether the simple hard-disagreement rule is a good choice. The rule drops 30% of digits at 20% noise and 50% at 40% noise, so roughly 13% of the clean digits samples are removed at 20% noise. Whether a thresholded variant drops fewer clean samples is the obvious question, and it is left open.
weaknesses.suggestion: Run confident-learning pruning and a kNN-based Wilson filter on the same 90-run grid. Add an oracle filter that drops exactly the flipped labels, which the authors can do since they know them. That gives an upper bound and shows how much of the remaining gap to clean accuracy comes from over-dropping.

weaknesses.issue: The statistical reading of breast cancer at 40% is inconsistent and partly wrong. The text says the filter's seed sd (9.0) exceeds its mean gain (3.6), so the gain cannot be told from 'a modest one'. But the seed sd of accuracy levels mostly reflects split and noise-draw variation shared by both methods. The relevant quantity is the sd of the paired differences, and the paired range is 2.3 to 5.8, positive in 5 of 5 seeds. Yet the same table counts 5/5 on digits as 'every seed' improvement and 4/5 on breast cancer at 20% as a result. There are no confidence intervals and no test, and with n=5 the strongest possible sign test has two-sided p=0.06. As a result, the paper's claims at 'clear' and 'unclear' levels are not backed by a common criterion.
weaknesses.where: Sec. 4 (Protocol, Metrics), Sec. 5.1 (last paragraph), abstract, Table 1
weaknesses.suggestion: Report the mean paired difference with its sd or a bootstrap/t interval for every row, and use that to define which results are 'clear'. Replace the level-sd comparison with the paired sd. Say plainly that 5 seeds are too few to separate small gains. Better, raise the seed count (repeated random splits are cheap on these datasets) so the claims are not decided by n=5.

weaknesses.issue: Recovery is the headline metric in the abstract and the intro, but it is a ratio of 5-seed means with the noisy-logreg gap in the denominator. It is unstable (the paper concedes this for breast cancer at 20%), and it has no uncertainty. It also uses clean-label logistic regression as the ceiling, which the filter does not have to reach, because the filter trains on fewer samples. Reporting '66%' and '22%' with no interval gives them more precision than 5 seeds allow.
weaknesses.suggestion: Move recovery out of the abstract, or give per-seed recovery with its range or a bootstrap interval. Lead with the paired accuracy difference, which is more robust and easier to read.

weaknesses.issue: The mechanistic account is not tested. The majority-vote argument with the bound eps<(k-1)/k is offered as explanation of the weaker breast-cancer result, and the paper says the 'small test and training sets are an alternative explanation that we did not test'. Breast cancer is also class-imbalanced and binary, so dropping samples may shift the class prior; the paper also says it did not measure per-class drop rates. Precision is quoted without the base rate: 76% precision at 40% noise on digits is a lift over a 39% flip rate, whereas 65% at 20% noise is a lift over 20%. 'Precision rises with noise' is partly a base-rate effect. The reading in Sec. 5.2 that the recall drop 'is consistent with' weaker recovery is not evidence for a cause.
weaknesses.suggestion: Report precision relative to the flip rate (lift), and the clean-sample drop rate as a share of the clean samples. Add per-class drop rates (the data already has them for digits at least). Check whether breast-cancer accuracy loss at 40% tracks class balance in the filtered set. Either test the binary-margin explanation (for example with a 3-class or imbalanced-subsampled variant) or reduce the claim to a conjecture.

weaknesses.issue: Only two small datasets, symmetric noise only, 5 seeds, and a 171-sample test set for breast cancer. The symmetric case is the one the majority argument favours, as the conclusion admits. No result involves class-dependent or instance-dependent noise, where out-of-fold disagreement can systematically remove hard but correctly labelled minority samples. The paper's 'logistic regression on small tabular data' framing therefore goes beyond what two sklearn toy datasets support.
weaknesses.suggestion: Add at least one asymmetric (pair-flip or class-dependent) noise setting and one or two more tabular datasets, if the compute allows. Otherwise restrict the claims, including the title, to 'symmetric noise on digits and breast cancer'.

weaknesses.issue: Hyperparameter claims conflict across sections. The abstract says 'no clean data, no noise rate and no confidence threshold; its settings ... were fixed and not tuned', which a reader may take as robust to settings. Sec. 3 says the filter is 'not setting-free' and the sensitivity to K and C is untested. The MLP baseline is also given no early stopping or regularization, and the MLP is never trained on filtered data, so the 'filter beats MLP by up to 27.7 points' is not a measurement of the filter's value but of a default MLP's memorization.
weaknesses.suggestion: Move the K/C caveat into the abstract. Show a small K and C sensitivity table (K in {3,5,10}, C in a few values). Train the MLP on the filtered data, or on an early-stopped MLP, so the MLP comparison says something about the filter.

questions: On breast cancer with clean labels, the MLP's mean and sd (96.7251 and 1.21266) are identical to those of logistic regression. Are the per-seed accuracies identical too? If so, is the MLP effectively reaching the same predictions on every test sample, or can a bug or shared model path explain it?
Does the filter's gain on digits at 20% noise persist when logistic regression uses C selected by cross-validation on the noisy labels?
What fraction of the clean training samples is dropped at 20% and 40% noise, per class? Do small or hard classes lose most?
Would a second pass of filtering (iterated) or a margin threshold keep the recall of 98% while lowering the 24-35% clean share among drops?
Are the splits, noise draws, and cross-validation fold shuffles drawn from separate random streams? The paper says a seed changes all of them together, so their variance is confounded.
